lead: Every die that leaves the fab looks the same from outside, yet some work and some do not. Test applies known inputs to each chip, reads its outputs and compares them with what a good chip gives, so bad parts are thrown out before a customer pays for them. Test costs a machine, a program and seconds per chip, so it must be planned. This chapter follows a chip from wafer to customer, names the steps where it is tested, and works out how yield and fault coverage decide how many bad chips still escape.
prereq: You need: the picture of a processed wafer full of identical die, from CMOS fabrication.

sections.h3: From wafer to chip, and where test sits

blocks.text: A chip is made in two halves. The front end builds transistors and wires on a silicon wafer: oxidation, lithography, etching, ion implantation and deposition, repeated layer by layer, then the metal interconnect. The back end turns tested die into parts.

items: Wafer fabrication: hundreds of identical die are built on one wafer.
Wafer probe (wafer sort): a probe card touches the bond pads of each die; failing die are marked on a wafer map.
Dicing and assembly: the wafer is sawn, good die are attached to a package and wire-bonded or flip-chip bonded, then sealed.
Burn-in (for parts that need it): hours of powered running at high temperature and voltage.
Final test: the packaged part runs the full test program, often at hot and cold temperature, and is sorted into bins.
Board and system test: after the part is soldered into a product (see 6.8).

blocks.text: Test is planned long before the wafer exists: in the design flow, test hardware (scan, BIST, boundary scan) is added after synthesis. Verification asks whether the design is right; test asks whether this copy was built right. A design can pass every simulation and still fail on the tester, because the fab made what the netlist never described: a short, an open, a missing contact. On a complex SoC both jobs are hard: too many states to simulate, too few pins to reach the inside, and cores that arrive with their own tests.

blocks.text: ATE, automatic test equipment, is the tester: pin electronics that drive and sense every chip pin, a precise timing generator, programmable power supplies and a computer that runs the test program.

items: DUT: the device under test, the chip being measured now.
Probe card: fine needles that land on the bond pads, so die are tested before packaging.
Device interface board (DIB): routes the tester channels to the socket or the probe card.
Handler: picks packaged chips from a tray, presses each into a socket at a set temperature, and drops it into a pass or fail bin.

sections.h3: Yield, fault coverage and defect level

blocks.text: Yield Y is the fraction of die that are free of killer defects and meet the specification. It falls as die area grows, because a random defect anywhere on a larger die kills it. A simple model with defects scattered at random is Y = e−A·D, where A is the die area and D the number of killer defects per unit area.

Fault coverage T is the fraction of the modelled faults that the test vectors detect. The faults come from a fault model (6.2) and T is measured by fault simulation (6.3). No real test program reaches T = 1.

blocks.where: where DL is the defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are bad; Y is the yield and T the fault coverage, both fractions between 0 and 1.
where DPM is defective parts per million shipped.

blocks.text: The formula (the Williams–Brown model) assumes defects are independent and that the test catches a fraction T of them, so (1 − T) escapes. Real defects cluster, so DL is an estimate, but as T rises towards 1 it falls steeply.

sections.h3: Quality, reliability and the four test stages

blocks.text: Quality describes parts at shipping: how many are bad, in DPM. Reliability describes parts after shipping: how long they keep working, in FIT, failures per 10⁹ device-hours.

The failure rate follows the bathtub curve: high and falling in the first weeks (infant mortality: weak oxide, bad vias), low in useful life, rising at wear-out (electromigration, oxide breakdown). Burn-in makes the infant failures happen in the factory.

A chip meets four kinds of test: silicon debug of first silicon on a bench; characterisation across voltage and temperature corners for the datasheet; production test of every chip on the ATE; and the customer's incoming inspection of a sample.

examples.question: A wafer lot has yield Y = 0.90. The production test program has fault coverage T = 0.95. (a) Find the defect level in DPM. (b) Repeat for a program with T = 0.99. (c) By what factor does the number of shipped bad parts fall?
steps: Formula: DL = 1 − Y<sup>(1 − T)</sup>. For (a), Y = 0.90 and 1 − T = 0.05.
Take logs to evaluate the power: ln 0.90 = −0.10536, and 0.05 × (−0.10536) = −0.005268.
Check: with T = 1 the exponent is 0, Y⁰ = 1 and DL = 0, so the numbers fall the right way as T rises.
examples.answer: About 5254 DPM at T = 0.95 and about 1053 DPM at T = 0.99, a fall by a factor of about 5 for 4 more points of coverage.

traps: Assuming 100 % fault coverage means zero escapes. T counts only the faults the model lists; a defect the model does not describe can still escape.
Swapping yield and fault coverage. Yield is a property of the fab (good die out of all die); fault coverage is a property of the test program (faults detected out of faults listed).
Mixing up the chain: a defect is physical, a fault is its logical model, an error is a wrong node value, a failure is lost function.
A unit slip in DPM: DL = 0.005 is 5000 DPM. Multiply by 10⁶, not 10⁴.
Saying verification proves the chip works. Simulation checks the design; only the tester checks each manufactured copy.

quiz.q: Define defect, fault, error and failure, one line each, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Defect: a physical flaw, such as a broken wire. Fault: its logical model, such as a line stuck at 0. Error: a wrong value at a node at some moment, such as 0110 instead of 0111. Failure: loss of the function the customer needs, such as a blank display.

quiz.q: Expand ATE, DUT and DIB, and say what a handler does.
quiz.a: Automatic test equipment, device under test, device interface board. The handler takes packaged chips from a tray, holds each in a socket at a set temperature, and sorts it into a pass bin or a fail bin.

quiz.q: List the steps from a processed wafer to a shipped chip, and mark the two steps that remove bad die.
quiz.a: Wafer fabrication, wafer probe, dicing and assembly, burn-in where needed, final test, shipping. Wafer probe removes bad die before packaging money is spent; final test removes parts that failed in assembly or burn-in, or at speed and temperature.

quiz.q: Distinguish quality from reliability and name the unit of each.
quiz.a: Quality is how many parts are bad at shipping, in DPM (defective parts per million). Reliability is how long parts keep working after shipping, in FIT (failures per 10⁹ device-hours).

quiz.q: A tester costs ₹0.60 per second to run. One die needs 2.5 s of test, and four die are tested in parallel. Find the test cost per die.
quiz.a: Cost per die = R × t ÷ s = 0.60 × 2.5 ÷ 4 = 1.50 ÷ 4 = ₹0.375, about 38 paise.

quiz.q: A lot has yield Y = 0.95 and the test program has fault coverage T = 0.90. Find the defect level and the DPM.
A team can afford one change: raise yield from 0.80 to 0.90, or raise coverage from 0.90 to 0.99. Use DL = 1 − Y<sup>(1 − T)</sup> to say which ships fewer bad parts.
quiz.a: Now: 1 − 0.80<sup>0.10</sup> = 0.02207, about 22,070 DPM. Yield only (Y = 0.90, T = 0.90): 1 − 0.90<sup>0.10</sup> = 0.01048, about 10,480 DPM, a 2.1 times fall. Coverage only (Y = 0.80, T = 0.99): 1 − 0.80<sup>0.01</sup> = 0.00223, about 2,230 DPM, a 9.9 times fall. Coverage wins here because it sits in the exponent: cutting (1 − T) from 0.10 to 0.01 shrinks the escape fraction ten-fold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Test engineering is a career of its own, and on large chips test cost is one of the biggest items after silicon area. Teams use defect-level models to argue how many vectors are worth paying for, and adaptive test uses earlier wafer and lot results to decide how long to test the next die. Search 'defect level Williams Brown', 'test cost model' and 'adaptive test semiconductor'.
